status_definitions.supported: Evidence supports the stated direction, sign, and reasoning within the declared scope.
status_definitions.partially_supported: Evidence supports only part of the claim, a narrower population or outcome, or an association rather than the full causal claim.
status_definitions.contradicted: Relevant evidence opposes the claimed direction or sign within the declared scope.
status_definitions.mixed_evidence: Relevant evidence both supports and opposes the same defined claim.
status_definitions.insufficient_evidence: Available evidence does not establish or refute the causal claim.
status_definitions.not_assessable: Undefined variable coding or endpoint makes the proposed direction or sign uninterpretable.

methodology.scope: 2010_8 yo.py, 58 edges, using 25 supplied PDFs (24 unique PDF documents) and 17 saved HTML article records. Two HTML records reproduce existing PDF studies: 39 unique documents total. Direction, sign, and written reasoning were reviewed; numeric strength was excluded.
methodology.age_scope: Evidence specific to children near age eight was preferred. Pediatric evidence with broader age ranges was treated as partial when it did not report an age-eight estimate. Adult-only evidence was not transferred to this graph.
methodology.causal_standard: Associations, reviews, and clinical recommendations were not automatically treated as proof of causal direction. Undefined categorical signs were marked not_assessable.
methodology.source_limits: This is a validation against the supplied corpus, not a systematic review of all 2010 ADHD literature. A status of insufficient_evidence is not evidence that an edge is false.
methodology.strength: The graph's numeric edge strengths were not validated.
methodology.duplicate: s12402-010-0036-9 (1).pdf is byte-identical to s12402-010-0036-9.pdf. The sex/age PubMed record (PMID 20410711) and ClinicalKey caudate article reproduce AGE_SEX and CAUDATE_MRI PDFs, respectively. Alternate formats are not independent studies.
methodology.html_scope: 15 PubMed records and two publisher records were parsed. Only primary article abstracts are used as new evidence; navigation, related articles and saved asset frames are excluded. ClinicalKey also contains the caudate full text, already supplied as PDF. Bipolar publication year is 2010 from the article date and journal citation, despite conflicting website citation metadata. Abstract encoding artifacts are preserved.
methodology.evidence_limits: Cross-sectional associations, selected prison/Tourette populations, clinical disparity commentary, and QOL endpoints are distinguished from causal exposure effects. QOL treatment gains do not validate diagnosis-only benefits or adverse-effect-only harm. Pediatric findings are not transferred to adult age-specific claims.

edges.existing_reasoning: Genetic liability contributes strongly to childhood ADHD.
edges.observation_from_validation: The corpus consistently describes ADHD as highly heritable. The large GWAS found no genome-wide significant individual variant, so the broad liability claim is supported more strongly than any specific genetic mechanism.
edges.recommended_action: Retain the positive edge, define Genetic Risk as aggregate inherited liability, and avoid implying a known single variant.

evidence.exact_excerpt: Although twin and family studies have shown attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) to be highly heritable, genetic variants influencing the trait at a genome-wide significant level have yet to be identified.
evidence.location: PDF page 1
evidence.relevance: Supports substantial inherited liability while cautioning that this GWAS did not identify individual genome-wide significant variants.

edges.existing_reasoning: Underlying ADHD increases symptom severity.
edges.observation_from_validation: ADHD and Symptom Severity overlap unless ADHD is defined as a latent liability separate from the symptoms used to diagnose it.
edges.recommended_action: Define a latent disorder construct and a separate severity measure before assigning a signed causal edge.

edges.existing_reasoning: Underlying ADHD shapes visible behavioral presentation.
edges.observation_from_validation: Symptom Type is categorical and has no ordered scale, so a universal positive sign is undefined.
edges.recommended_action: Use category-specific outcomes or an unsigned relationship.

edges.existing_reasoning: At age 8, symptoms are highly visible through behavior and school functioning.
edges.observation_from_validation: The supplied age analysis shows prevalence and symptom patterns varying with age, but 'age eight is highly visible' is not a positive slope from age to severity.
edges.recommended_action: Replace the plus sign with an age-specific function or explicit comparison.

evidence.exact_excerpt: Overall prevalence of current DSM-IV-like ADHD was 9.2% with a male:female ratio of 2.28:1. The prevalence of DSM-IV-like ADHD was highest in children. Gender differences in DSM-IV-like ADHD subtype prevalences were highest in adolescents.
evidence.location: PDF page 1
evidence.relevance: Shows age and sex differences in prevalence and subtype patterns, not the graph's proposed social-norm mechanism.

edges.existing_reasoning: Gender norms influence which childhood behaviors are noticed.
edges.observation_from_validation: The evidence shows sex differences in subtype prevalence and possible underdiagnosis of females, but Symptom Type is unordered and the proposed gender-norm mechanism was not tested.
edges.recommended_action: Specify sex or gender, a presentation contrast, and the proposed detection mechanism.

evidence.exact_excerpt: Overall prevalence of current DSM-IV-like ADHD was 9.2% with a male:female ratio of 2.28:1. The prevalence of DSM-IV-like ADHD was highest in children. Gender differences in DSM-IV-like ADHD subtype prevalences were highest in adolescents.

evidence.exact_excerpt: Lower male:female ratios than reported in some clinic-based studies suggest that females are under-diagnosed in the community.
evidence.location: PDF page 1
evidence.relevance: Supports unequal detection by sex but does not isolate teacher referral or institutional bias.

edges.existing_reasoning: Early nutrition can modulate developmental vulnerability.
edges.observation_from_validation: Inherited liability is not an ordered outcome that better nutrition can simply reduce; no paper tests nutrition changing genetic risk.
edges.recommended_action: Model nutrition as a possible modifier of expression, not as a cause of inherited liability.

edges.existing_reasoning: Poor nutrition may worsen behavioral regulation.
edges.observation_from_validation: The added nutritional review abstract describes topics and the need to scrutinize study validity, but reports no treatment-effect conclusion. It cannot validate better general nutrition reducing ADHD symptom severity.
edges.recommended_action: Obtain the full review or directly relevant nutritional-intervention results; keep general nutrition separate from individual supplements or elimination diets.

evidence.exact_excerpt: This updated review presents the evidence regarding the usefulness and limitations of the most frequent nutritional and dietary interventions in the treatment of ADHD and/or ASD.
evidence.location: Effectiveness of nutritional interventions on the functioning of children with ADHD and_or ASD. An updated review of research evidence - PubMed.html; article abstract (#eng-abstract)
evidence.relevance: Abstract describes the review scope but supplies no efficacy conclusion, effect size or comparison supporting the direction of the nutrition edge.

edges.existing_reasoning: Better sleep reduces dysregulation.
edges.observation_from_validation: The existing actigraphy-duration association near ages seven–eight remains relevant. The added study finds parent-reported sleep problems associated with behavior but no polysomnographic group differences. It strengthens measurement and direction cautions rather than establishing a causal sleep-to-severity effect.
edges.recommended_action: Keep the qualified sleep association; identify the sleep measure, informant and uncertain direction. Do not label different sleep measures as contradictory tests of one causal intervention.

evidence.exact_excerpt: shorter sleep duration in 7- to 8 year olds (as measured by actigraphy) was associated with increased caregiver reports of inattentive/hyperactive problem behavior.
evidence.location: PDF page 2
evidence.relevance: Directly relevant to age eight, but observational wording supports association rather than a fully identified causal effect.

evidence.exact_excerpt: There is some evidence of a causal relationship between sleep disruption and difficulties regulating behavior, emotion, and attention. However, such associations have rarely been experimentally evaluated, because the majority of sleep studies have used correlational designs.
evidence.location: PDF page 2
evidence.relevance: The review itself states both the plausible direction and the causal limitation.

evidence.exact_excerpt: However, there were no differences between ADHD and healthy groups on any polysomnographic variables, including sleep structure, arousals, and respiratory disturbances.
evidence.location: Differences between objective and subjective sleep measures in children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder - PubMed.html; article abstract (#eng-abstract)
evidence.relevance: Unmedicated children aged 7–12; objective group comparisons differed from parental sleep reports. No intervention on sleep or causal severity effect.

evidence.exact_excerpt: Reported sleep problems were significantly associated with almost all subscales of CBCL as well as CBCL total score.
evidence.location: Differences between objective and subjective sleep measures in children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder - PubMed.html; article abstract (#eng-abstract)
evidence.relevance: Subjective sleep-behavior association; shared informant effects and reverse direction remain possible. This does not negate the earlier actigraphy-duration association.

edges.existing_reasoning: Environmental stressors can worsen symptoms.
edges.observation_from_validation: The existing prenatal organochlorine association is supplemented by lifetime lead associated with recorded pediatric ADHD diagnosis. Both are exposure-specific observational evidence, not generic stressor effects on severity.
edges.recommended_action: Specify contaminant, timing and endpoint; retain confounding and ascertainment limitations.

evidence.exact_excerpt: These results support an association between low-level prenatal organochlorine exposure and ADHD-like behaviors in childhood.
evidence.location: PDF page 1
evidence.relevance: Supports a specific prenatal exposure association, narrower than the graph's generic environmental-stressor claim.

evidence.exact_excerpt: elevated lead remained a significant predictor of ADHD diagnosis in multivariate analysis.
evidence.location: Geographic analysis of diagnosis of Attention-Deficit_Hyperactivity Disorder in children_ Eastern Wisconsin, USA - PubMed.html; article abstract (#eng-abstract)
evidence.relevance: Lifetime lead association with recorded pediatric diagnosis; not proof of generic environmental stressor effects on symptom severity.

edges.existing_reasoning: More severe symptoms increase impairment.
edges.observation_from_validation: Existing ADHD–impairment context is supplemented by psychosocial/educational problems in a selected Tourette sample with ADHD/OCD comorbidity. The new association does not identify an independent symptom-severity causal gradient.
edges.recommended_action: Keep population-specific functional context separate from a causal severity effect.

evidence.exact_excerpt: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a highly prevalent disorder with significant functional impairment.
evidence.location: PDF page 1
evidence.relevance: Links ADHD and impairment, but does not independently estimate symptom-severity-to-impairment causation.

evidence.exact_excerpt: A higher rate of these problems was also seen if the comorbidities attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and/or obsessive compulsive disorder were present.
evidence.location: The presence of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and obsessive-compulsive disorder worsen psychosocial and educational problems in Tourette syndrome - PubMed.html; article abstract (#eng-abstract)
evidence.relevance: Selected Tourette pediatric sample: psychosocial and educational problems correlate with comorbidity; school support need is not evidence that ADHD diagnosis causes formal accommodations.

edges.existing_reasoning: Certain symptom patterns are likely to trigger teacher concern.
edges.observation_from_validation: Symptom Type has no ordered coding, and no supplied study estimates teacher referral rates by presentation.
edges.recommended_action: Define a specific presentation contrast and a referral denominator.

edges.existing_reasoning: By 2010, school resources strongly support detection.
edges.observation_from_validation: The geographic study shows differences in recorded pediatric diagnoses, and the commentary proposes access/referral contributors. Neither measures this specific graph exposure-to-outcome effect; geographic or racial diagnosis differences alone do not establish provider availability, institutional bias, or referral causation.
edges.recommended_action: Retain as unvalidated; measure the named exposure and endpoint directly rather than substituting recorded diagnosis distribution.

evidence.exact_excerpt: Conclusions: Further studies are needed to determine if geographic distribution of ADHD diagnosis can be partially explained by differential efficiency of referral for diagnosis by school districts, by race/ethnicity, and/or built environment.

evidence.relevance: Observational children aged 5–17; diagnosis differences do not identify institutional bias, provider access or school-referral efficiency as the causal mechanism.
